source.title: ALLaM: Large Language Models for Arabic and English
source.authors: M Saiful Bari; Yazeed Alnumay; Norah A. Alzahrani; Nouf M. Alotaibi; H. Alyahya; Sultan Alrashed; F. Mirza; Shaykhah Z. Alsubaie; Hassan A. Alahmed; Ghadah Alabduljabbar; Raghad Alkhathran; Yousef Almushayqih; Raneem Alnajim; Salman Alsubaihi; Maryam Al Mansour; Majed Alrubaian; Ali Alammari; Zaki Alawami; A. Al-Thubaity; Ahmed Abdelali; Jeril Kuriakose; Abdalghani Abujabal; Nora Al-Twairesh; Areeb Alowisheq; Haidar Khan

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures downstream benchmark performance during pretraining across model sizes and training-token progress, which bears conceptually on downstream performance scaling. It does not fit or reproduce the original held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. and discusses scaling laws, but reports no held-out cross-entropy scaling fits, small-run forecasts, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture-shape sweep. Figure 10 reports the paper's own downstream benchmark trajectories during mixed Arabic/English pretraining and is included. Figure 2 compares benchmark results across different models but does not establish a fitted scaling relation, so it is not included as a result row.
record.test_reason: This is a model-release report for ALLaM. It cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. only in passing, in the introduction and when justifying token counts. It fits no loss or downstream scaling relation and tests no forecast. Figure 10 tracks benchmarks during mixed Arabic/English continued pretraining at four model sizes, which is a language-shift and capacity observation rather than a test of predictable scaling. Size is also confounded with training: the 70B model saw only 600B mixed tokens versus 1.2T for the others, and the 7B from-scratch model has a different history. The reader's V6 link and labels are not justified.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that ALLaM reaches state-of-the-art Arabic benchmark results while maintaining or improving English. They attribute this to vocabulary expansion and mixed Arabic/English continued pretraining, which give second-language acquisition without catastrophic forgetting. They also credit translated data for aiding alignment and conclude that careful human-preference alignment lets ALLaM beat larger models. Incidentally, in Figure 10 smaller models trade off between languages while 70B improves in both. They draw no conclusions about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates benchmark trajectories of its own Arabic-English models; it does not fit held-out-loss laws or perform the original scaling-law prediction and compute-allocation analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with model size: smaller models degrade when Arabic is introduced, whereas the 70B model can improve in both languages.

fits_no_version.finding: During training, HellaSwag improves smoothly, while GSM8K improves in discontinuous jumps and other benchmarks show no gain until about 1.5T tokens. This is stated qualitatively in Section 4.1 with no figure or numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream benchmarks differ in smoothness of improvement over training tokens; some show delayed, jump-like gains (a training-progress analogue of V6 limits).

fits_no_version.finding: In mixed Arabic/English continued pretraining, smaller models trade off English HellaSwag for Arabic, while the 70B model improves in both languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model capacity determines whether adding a second language causes forgetting in the first language.

record.problems: Figure 10's trajectories are presented without numerical values in the text or reported uncertainty. The study does not perform predictive tests or fit scaling relations.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2's cross-model benchmark-versus-parameter-size plot is not catalogued because it does not report a fitted or tested scaling relation. No additional Figure 10 rows were omitted.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes; continued pretraining is not analysed for scaling form.
No fitted or predicted relation between scale or loss and downstream accuracy. Figure 10 and the remarks on smooth versus jumpy benchmarks are qualitative and confounded by language shift.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader overreached by treating benchmark trajectories during continued pretraining as a V6 test. Figure 2 compares different models and so is rightly excluded. The 1B small-scale bilingual-from-scratch observation is anecdotal and has no data.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Forecasting much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Comparisons isolating depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Scaling-law form in other modalities or the specified repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer settings.
The paper reports downstream benchmark trajectories during pretraining, but does not fit a predictive relation, test forecasts, or relate downstream performance to pretraining loss.
Whether law exponents or compute-optimal allocation vary with fitting choices, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: ALLaM smaller models (reported group: 7B, 13B, and 7B from scratch)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked benchmark performance during mixed Arabic/English pretraining

conditions.value: Arabic introduced during mixed Arabic/English pretraining

rows.value: figure only; the text says smaller models' performance degrades when Arabic is introduced
rows.note: The paper identifies HellaSwag as a proxy for language understanding. The figure does not provide numerical values in the text.
rows.check: HellaSwag degradation in smaller models when Arabic is introduced measures forgetting under a distribution shift, not downstream predictability with scale or loss. It is figure-only with no numbers, and no fitted or predicted relation exists.

rows.subject: ALLaM 70B
rows.operation_detail: Tracked benchmark performance during mixed Arabic/English pretraining
rows.value: figure only; the text says the 70B model can improve in English while acquiring Arabic
rows.note: No numeric trajectory values are stated in the text.
rows.check: English MMLU improvement for 70B during mixed-language continued pretraining is a capacity and forgetting observation for a single model. It does not test whether downstream performance tracks scale or loss predictably. Figure-only.

rows.subject: ALLaM 70B
rows.operation_detail: Tracked benchmark performance during mixed Arabic/English pretraining
rows.value: figure only; the text says the 70B model can improve in Arabic while retaining or improving English performance
rows.note: No numeric trajectory values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Arabic MMLU rise for 70B during continued pretraining is new-language acquisition and is figure-only. No scaling relation is tested.

rows.subject: ALLaM models (aggregate stated for all models)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked Arabic benchmark performance during pretraining
rows.value: figure only; the text describes Arabic acquisition as rapid in all models
rows.note: The paper states this as an aggregate result for all models; it gives no exact trajectory values in the text.
rows.check: The claim that Arabic acquisition is rapid in all models is qualitative and figure-only. It shows no size-dependent or loss-dependent predictable trend, and sizes are confounded with token counts (70B trained on 600B vs 1.2T tokens).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ALLaM 70B and Arabic MMLU trajectories across the tested models
reader_labels.reason: The reported benchmark trajectories show simultaneous English/Arabic improvement for ALLaM 70B and rapid Arabic acquisition across models (r2, r3, r4); the paper does not establish quantitative predictability.
